Section 2: Four-Cycle Engine Theory Introduction If the engine is to run properly, four events must occur in proper sequence and at the correct time. These events are (A) intake, (B) compression, (C) ignition and power, and (D) exhaust. (A) Intake (C) Power Four-Cycle Engine Theory 001684 The piston is traveling from top dead center (TDC) to bottom dead center (BDC). The cam has opened the intake valve. The piston's downward movement in the cylinder creates a partial vacuum in the cylinder. Air at atmospheric pressure is drawn into the cylinder through the carburetor and is mixed with fuel in the carburetor. The fuel-air mixture flows through the open intake valve into the cylinder. When the piston reaches BDC, the intake stroke is over. (B) Compression 001686 By the time the piston reaches TDC, combustion is already in progress. The intake and exhaust valves remain closed as the expanding gases of combustion force the piston downward. (D) Exhaust 001687 The exhaust stroke begins when the piston has reached BDC and has started its upward movement. The intake valve is closed. The exhaust valve is open to let gases escape. 001685 As the piston reaches bottom dead center (BDC), both the intake and exhaust valves are closed. The piston moves upward toward TDC and the fuel-air mixture is compressed. Just before the piston reaches TDC, ignition occurs. OHVI® V-Twin Engine Service Manual 9

Fuel And Oil Recommendations Gasoline Use clean, fresh lead-free gasoline with a minimum of 85 octane. Lead-free gasoline results in fewer combustion deposits and longer valve life. NOTE: A fuel additive such as Sta-Bil® fuel stabilizer, or an equivalent, will prevent gum deposits from forming in the engine fuel system. NOTE: Some fuels, called oxygenated or reformulated gasolines, are gasolines blended with alcohols or ethers. Excessive amounts of these blends can damage the fuel system or cause performance problems. Do not use gasoline which contains Methanol. If any undesirable operating symptoms occur, use gasoline with a lower percentage of alcohol or ether. Recommended percentage is 10% or less. Gasoline should be purchased in small quantities–not more than a 30 day supply. Fresh gasoline minimizes gum deposits, and also ensures fuel volatility tailored for the season in which the engine will be operated. Lubrication Oil has four purposes—it cools, cleans, seals, and lubricates. During normal operation, small particles of metal from the cylinder walls, pistons, bearings, and combustion deposits gradually contaminate oil. Dust particles from the air also contaminate oil, forming an abrasive mixture which causes wear to all of the internal moving parts of the engine if oil is not changed regularly. Fresh oil also assists in cooling. Old oil gradually becomes thick and loses its cooling ability and lubricating qualities. Recommended Oil Proper crankcase oil type and oil weight is extremely important. Check oil before each use and change oil regularly (see Figure 3-2 through Figure 3-6). Incorrect or dirty oil can cause premature engine wear and failure. Use only high quality detergent oil rated with API service classification SN or higher. Recommended oil weights include the following: • During summer months: SAE 30. An acceptable substitute is SAE 10W-30. After first oil change, synthetic oil is acceptable. • During winter months: SAE 5W-30 or Synthetic 5W- 30. DO NOT USE SAE 10W-40. After first oil change, synthetic oil is acceptable. 10W-30 SAE 30 Synthetic 5W-30 Figure 3-1. Recommended Oil 000399 OHVI® V-Twin Engine Service Manual 11

Troubleshooting Most complaints concerning engine operation can be classified as one or a combination of the following: • Will not start • Hard starting • Lack of power • Runs rough • Vibration • Overheating • High oil consumption NOTE: What appears to be an engine malfunction may be a fault of the powered equipment rather than the engine. If equipment is suspect, see Equipment Affecting Engine Operation. Systematic Check If the engine will not start and the cause of malfunction is not readily apparent, perform a systematic check in the following order: 1. Fuel 2. Ignition 3. Compression These checks, performed in a systematic manner, can usually be done in a matter of minutes. It is the quickest and surest method of determining the cause of failure. The basic check procedure is the same for all engine models. Any variation, by model, will be described under the subject heading. Check Fuel Fuel pressure on LP and NG generator engines can be checked using a pressure test kit for LP and NG systems. For gasoline engines, check the following: • Are tanks full? • Is fuel stale? • Is tank vent open? • Is fuel shutoff valve open? • Is fuel pump working? • Is fuel solenoid working? Check Compression The following procedure is a simple and accurate test of cylinder compression. 1. Remove both spark plugs and insert a compression gauge into either cylinder (one cylinder at a time). 2. Open throttle to Wide Open Throttle (WOT) position. 3. Turn engine over with engine starter until there is no further increase in pressure. Record this reading. 4. Repeat procedure on other cylinder and record that reading. The difference between both cylinders should not exceed 25%. More than 25% indicates loss of compression in the cylinder with lower pressure. To calculate the difference in percentage, divide the difference in PSI (kPa) by the higher pressure reading. Refer to the examples below. A cylinder leakdown test indicates cylinder condition. It will assist in troubleshooting leaking valves or rings. See Figure 3-11. There are two gauges on the tester. One measures incoming air pressure, and the other measures the percent of cylinder leakage. Testing Procedure 1. Align piston at TDC. 2. Install tester in the spark plug hole. 3. Equipment Affecting Engine Operation Frequently, what appears to be a problem with engine operation, such as hard starting or vibration, may be the fault of the equipment being powered rather than the engine itself. Listed are the most common effects of equipment problems—and what to look for as the most common cause. Hard Starting or Will Not Start • Loose drive mechanism—A loose drive mechanism (for example, a belt), can cause a backlash effect which will counteract engine cranking effort. • Starting under load—Observe if unit is disengaged when engine starts; or, if engaged, unit should not have a heavy starting load. • Check remote control assembly for proper adjustment. • Check interlock system for shorted wires, loose or corroded connections, or defective modules or switches. Engine Will Not Stop • Check equipment ignition stop switch. • Check for loose or disconnected equipment stop switch wire. • Check ground wire harness on engine. • See Ignition for test procedure. Vibration • Unit load out of balance—remove and balance. • Mounting bolts loose—tighten. Power Loss • Bind or drag in unit. If possible, disengage engine and operate unit manually to feel for any binding action. • Unit load has excess drag. Noise • Engine coupling or pulley. An oversize or worn coupling can result in knocking, usually under acceleration. Check for fit or tightness. • Equipment needs lubrication. OHVI® V-Twin Engine Service Manual General Information 17

Ignition Section 4: Ignition Overview Generac GTH/GTV-999 OHVI V-Twin engines use a magneto ignition, which is an ignition coil with a selfcontained transistor module (no moving parts). Two magneto ignition coils are used, with a flywheel containing a permanent magnet. NOTE: The magneto ignition system requires a minimum of 250 rpm to produce a consistent spark. Ignition Check If the engine runs but misses during operation, first check to determine if the ignition system is functioning properly. 1. See Figure 4-7. Install a spark tester (B) between the spark plug lead (A) and each spark plug (C) as shown. Test each plug separately if only one spark tester is available. A B Ignition Coil Test Test ignition coil if the ignition check indicates one or both of the coils are not delivering a strong consistent spark. 1. Remove ground wire from ignition ground stud on the back side of the blower housing (oil filter side). 2. Repeat ignition check procedure to determine if ignition now has spark. 3. If spark is present, check wiring harness for broken insulation or pinched wires. These faults may cause a ground contact in the circuit between the grounding stud and the low oil pressure switch or engine kill switch. 4. If there is no spark present, then proceed with Coil Diode Test. NOTE: Verify engine has oil and there is no continuity between the two spade lugs on the low oil pressure switch while cranking or during operation. Continuity between the spade lugs indicates low or nonexistent oil pressure, or a faulty low oil pressure switch. The low oil pressure switch will ground the coils if <10 psig (69 kPa) is present at the switch; stopping the engine. C 004297 Figure 4-1. Spark Tester on Engine (Typical) 2. Start engine and verify if a steady spark is visible in the window of the tester. A lack of spark or miss will be readily apparent when the engine is running, indicating further investigation of the ignition system is required. 3. If spark is steady for both cylinders but engine still misses or will not run, check for a fouled spark plug. Also, verify fuel is present in the carburetor and power is being supplied to the fuel shut-off solenoid. OHVI® V-Twin Engine Service Manual 19

Carburetion and Fuel System Section 5: Carburetion and Fuel System Carburetion Overview Proper engine performance depends on the carburetion system. Clean, fresh fuel and a well maintained air cleaner are extremely important to engine operation, engine reliability, and power. All Generac gasoline powered OHVI V-Twin engines feature a two-barrel type carburetor. Some LP engines use a single barrel carburetor. Common Carburetor Problems Most carburetor problems are related to the use of stale, gummy fuel and dirt ingestion. Check for evidence of these conditions before servicing any carburetor. Gasoline left in the fuel system for long periods can form gum or varnish deposits adversely affecting carburetor operation. NOTE: A reliable fuel stabilizer (available from an IASD) will minimize the formation of gum deposits during storage. Add stabilizer to the gasoline in the fuel tank or storage container. Follow the mix ratio recommended on the stabilizer container. After adding stabilizer to the engine fuel tank, run the engine for about 10 minutes to draw stabilized fuel through the carburetor. Service Tip Carefully inspect carburetor choke and throttle shafts for wear. Grasp each shaft and attempt to move it horizontally and vertically. Maximum allowable end play for choke and throttle shafts is 0.004 in (0.1 mm). Replace if excessive play is evident. OHVI® V-Twin Engine Service Manual 27

Section 8:Electric Starter Electric Starter General Information See Figure 8-1. The starter motor utilizes a solenoid, similar to an automobile starter, to assist in pinion gear engagement. When the starter motor is activated, the pinion gear engages a ring gear attached to the engine flywheel and cranks the engine. Figure 8-1. Starter Motor 004057 Troubleshooting NOTE: If a starting problem is encountered, check the engine thoroughly to eliminate it as the cause of starting difficulty. Check engine for free rotation by removing spark plugs and flywheel guard and turning the crankshaft with a socket and ratchet or breaker bar. Verify it rotates freely. WARNING: Do not rotate engine with electric starter while spark plugs are removed, unless using a compression gauge. Arcing at the spark plug ends may ignite gasoline vapor exiting the spark plug hole. Engine cranks slowly: • Additional load affecting performance (see note above). • Discharged battery. • Faulty electrical connection (battery circuit). • Discharged battery (see alternators). • Dirty or worn starter motor commutator, bearing, weak magnets, etc. • Worn brushes or weak brush spring. • Wrong oil viscosity for temperature expected. • Battery leads too long or wire too small. • Underpowered battery. Engine will not crank: • Faulty safety interlocks. • Discharged or defective battery. • Faulty electrical connections. • Faulty starter motor switch (open circuit). • Open circuit in starter motor. • Brushes sticking, etc. • Faulty solenoid. Starter motor spins but does not crank engine: • Sticking pinion gear due to dirt. • Damaged pinion or ring gear. • Battery faulty or damaged. • Incorrect rotation due to reversed motor polarity — all motors rotate counterclockwise viewed from pinion gear. • Damaged solenoid. Starter motor spins but will not stop: • Defective starter switch. • Solenoid stuck engaged. Test Equipment Digital Multimeter (DMM) See Figure 8-2. Section 9: Lubrication System Lubrication System Description Generac GTH/GTV-760/990 OHVI V-twins use a full pressure lubrication system with an oil filter. A gerotor oil pump draws oil from a screened oil pickup in the sump and pumps oil through the oil filter. Filtered oil flows through an oil gallery in the sump and is distributed to the main bearings, connecting rod bearings, and camshaft bearings. Engine oil pressure varies with oil viscosity, ambient air temperature differences, operating temperatures and engine load. See Recommended Oil Type. Oil Pressure - @ 70 °F (21 °C): 15–50 psi (103–345 kPa) Two pressure relief valves limit the maximum oil pressure in the system to 60 and 40 psi (414–276 kPa) respectively. Protection Systems Low Oil Pressure Switch See Figure 9-1. The engine is usually equipped with a normally open type, low oil pressure switch (A) which closes the circuit between the terminals when oil pressure drops below 8 psi (55 kPa). If one terminal is connected to the ignition ground wire and the other terminal is connected to ground, the engine will shut down on low oil pressure. The switch can also be connected to an alarm or light to indicate low oil pressure, instead of shutting down the engine. NOTE: Some engine models have a normally closed type switch and work the opposite as above. A A delay built into the shutdown system on some engine applications allows oil pressure to build during starting. The delay allows the engine to run for about 10 seconds before sensing oil pressure. If the engine is wired for low oil pressure shutdown and the system senses low oil pressure during operation, the engine shuts down. The engine will not run until 8 psi (55 kPa) of oil pressure is reached. If a restart is attempted within five seconds after shutdown, the engine may NOT start. The system needs 10 seconds to reset. Check Engine Oil Level Oil capacity of the GTH/GTV-760/990 OHVI engine is approximately 2 qt (1.9L). See Recommended Oil Type.for the proper amount for each model. Avoid honing cylinder bores oversize. Oversize cylinder bores will permanently damage the crankcase. See Figure 11-4. Special honing stones are required when reconditioning a cylinder bore. Honing stones produce the correct cross hatch necessary for proper lubrication and ring seating. Honing is performed as a two step process called plateau honing. These steps must be followed carefully and should be performed by a competent machine shop. The correct cross hatch angle is approximately 45 degrees. 45º Figure 11-4. Cylinder Cross Hatch 004359 Honing is done with a variable speed half-inch portable drill and a honing fixture. Figure 11-6 at the end of this topic provides dimensions for making a honing fixture. Setup 1. See Figure 11-5. Use two crankcase cover mounting screws to fasten honing fixture (A) to crankcase. A Figure 11-5. Honing Cylinders 004360 2. Cut a wood block and place inside crankcase to prevent hone from extending further than 0.75–1.0 in (19 mm–25 mm) below cylinder bore. 3. For the first pass, hone each cylinder with a 220 grit diamond metal-bond super-abrasive stone (such as a Sunnen® GMG55). Set drill speed at 240 rpm at 80 strokes per minute. Lubricate cylinder liberally to prevent buildup on honing stones. 2. For the second pass, hone each cylinder with an 800 grit diamond metal-bond super-abrasive stone (such as a Sunnen® RMG807) at 110 rpm drill speed at 80 strokes per minute. NOTE: Sunnen® lubricating oil (SCC605) is recommended. Automatic transmission fluid is also an acceptable honing oil. Another acceptable honing oil can be made by mixing four parts 30 weight oil with one part kerosene. Cleaning Clean each cylinder and crankcase thoroughly after honing. 1. Wash cylinder and crankcase carefully in a commercial solvent or kerosene. 2. Thoroughly wash cylinder and crankcase using a stiff brush with soap and hot water. Rinse thoroughly with hot running water. 3. Repeat washing and rinsing until all traces of honing grit are gone. IMPORTANT NOTE: Honing grit is highly abrasive and will cause rapid wear to all internal components of the engine unless it is completely removed. 4. When cylinder and crankcase have been thoroughly cleaned, use a clean white rag or paper towel and wipe the cylinder bore. Any remaining honing grit will be visible as a gray residue. If any honing grit is evident, wash and rinse entire cylinder and crankcase, and check again. The cylinder is properly cleaned when there is no trace of honing grit on the rag. Section 14: Troubleshooting Troubleshooting Problem Solving Introduction Problems affecting engine operation may be classified as one of, or a combination of two or more of, the following: • Engine will not start. • Engine starts with difficulty. • Engine lacks power. • Engine vibrates. • Engine overheats. • Engine burns oil. In many cases, the cause will be readily apparent. If this is not the case, check the fuel system, ignition system, and engine compression. These checks can be performed quickly and are the best methods of finding the cause of a failure. They may also predict future failures. Check Fuel System Verify fuel tank has been properly filled with correct fuel. If engine is equipped with a fuel shutoff valve, confirm valve is open. Verify fuel is flowing through fuel line and to carburetor. Adjust carburetor as needed. Verify choke closes all the way. If engine does not start, remove and inspect spark plug. If spark plug is WET, look for the following: • Overchoking. • Dirty air cleaner. • Excessively rich fuel-air mixture. • Water in fuel. • Fuel leaking past carburetor float needle. If spark plug is DRY, look for the following: • Carburetor mounting gasket leaks. • Dirt or gum in carburetor or fuel line. • Carburetor float needle stuck closed. • Inoperative fuel pump (if equipped). • Clogged fuel filter (if equipped). Check Ignition System See testing procedures in section Ignition. Check Compression To check engine compression: 1. Remove spark plug. 2. Insert an automotive type compression gauge into the spark plug hole. 3. Crank engine until there is no further increase in pressure. The highest reading obtained is engine compression pressure. If compression is poor, look for one or more of the following causes: • Loose cylinder head bolts. • Failed cylinder head gasket. • Burned valves or valve seats. • Insufficient valve clearance. • Warped cylinder head. • Warped valve stem. • Worn or broken piston ring(s). • Worn or damaged cylinder bore. • Broken connecting rod. • Worn valve seats or valves. • Worn valve guides.
